tagline: Post-Olympics Paris is doubling down on what it does best — pedestrianized streets, a swimmable Seine and a freshly restored Notre-Dame. It is ranked #22 on Time Out's Best Cities 2026 list.
overview: Paris emerged from its 2024 Olympics summer with real momentum. The Games turned the city into the venue — beach volleyball under the Eiffel Tower, fencing in the Grand Palais — and left behind the most visible legacy of all: a swimmable Seine, with public river-bathing sites opened in summer 2025.

The bigger story is the rebuilt heart of the city. Notre-Dame reopened in December 2024, five years after the fire, its restored interior drawing enormous crowds (reserve the free timed entry slot online). Around it, Mayor Hidalgo’s pedestrian makeover has become permanent: the Rue de Rivoli runs largely car-free, the Seine’s banks belong to walkers and cyclists, a citywide 30 km/h speed limit is in force, and thousands of former parking spots are caf’ terraces by law.

The classics are untouched by time: the Louvre and its pyramid, the Mus’e d’Orsay, the Luxembourg Gardens, and a dining scene that rewards every arrondissement — from a €2 baguette to three-star tasting menus.

One tip for 2026: Paris is busier than ever in peak season. Visit in the shoulder months (April–May or late September–October), book the big museums online in advance, and let the M’tro and your feet do the rest — the city is more walkable now than at any point in its modern history.

funFacts.title: Paris has several Statues of Liberty
funFacts.text: The most famous Statue of Liberty is in New York, but Paris has several smaller replicas, including one on the Île aux Cygnes in the Seine.

funFacts.title: Home of the Mona Lisa
funFacts.text: The Louvre, the world's most visited art museum, houses Leonardo da Vinci's Mona Lisa, perhaps the most famous painting in the world.

funFacts.title: 20 arrondissements
funFacts.text: Paris is divided into 20 districts called arrondissements, which spiral out clockwise from the centre like a snail shell.

funFacts.title: A city beneath the city
funFacts.text: Under Paris lie the Catacombs, old quarry tunnels that hold the remains of millions of Parisians moved there in the late 1700s.

funFacts.title: Why it's the City of Light
funFacts.text: Paris earned the name City of Light as one of the first European cities to light its streets on a large scale, starting under Louis XIV in the 17th century. The name also nods to its role in the Enlightenment.

funFacts.title: Two natural islands
funFacts.text: The Seine has two natural islands in the heart of Paris: the Île de la Cité, home to Notre-Dame Cathedral, and the Île Saint-Louis. Both are linked to the rest of the city by bridges.

funFacts.title: The Bloody Mary was born here
funFacts.text: The Bloody Mary cocktail is said to have been first mixed in the 1920s at Harry's New York Bar in Paris.

funFacts.title: Love locks didn't start in Paris
funFacts.text: Paris made love locks famous, but the tradition is often traced to the Serbian town of Vrnjačka Banja, where a story of lost love led couples to lock padlocks on a bridge.

funFacts.title: Almost no stop signs
funFacts.text: Paris is famous for having almost no stop signs. Drivers rely on traffic lights and the priority-to-the-right rule instead.

funFacts.title: Over 450 parks and gardens
funFacts.text: Paris has more than 450 parks and gardens, perfect for picnics. The best known are the Tuileries Garden and the Luxembourg Gardens.
